title: The Gurus' teachings close
hook: five Gurus, one signature: looking back at Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan and Tegh Bahadur

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Name that remains, when Ram and Ravan have gone. Your line was it remains. When something ended, did you remember once more? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

Here's a small thing on the page that's easy to miss. When the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, they use one name: Nanak. Guru Angad signs as Nanak. Guru Amar Das signs as Nanak. So do Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, and the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. How do readers tell them apart? Above each hymn sits a heading: Mahala, with a number. Mahala one, two, three, four, five, nine. Different hands, different generations of the same story, one name. Today we close this whole stretch of the path by listening to them all at once.
screen: `ONE SIGNATURE: NANAK.` → `MAHALA ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR, FIVE, NINE.` → `LISTEN TO THEM ALL AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Start with Guru Angad, the quiet successor. Few words, deep. He called the Guru a light where all was dark, warned against service mixed with pride, and called ego an illness with the cure inside it. Short and sharp. Then Guru Amar Das, the old Guru's voice. O mind, you are the form of light. The world is burning; save it by any door. Not the pyre, but a faithful life. And a kitchen open to all. Then Guru Ram Das. The Gursikh's morning: rising early, remembering, then going to work still remembering. Wedding songs of the soul riding to the Beloved. A city where the market itself could be holy. Then Guru Arjan. An alphabet that ends in grace. A plate of three things: truth, contentment, reflection. What You do seems sweet to me. Serving the One. And a book, chosen carefully, with room for saints from outside the line of Gurus. And last, the ninth Guru. Neither fear nor frighten. Home, held lightly. Their faith, their right. Level. A dream, a bubble, and the Name that remains. Hear how different they sound. A spare one-liner. A burning world. A wedding song. A long alphabet. A calm verse that tradition hears through his last days. And yet it's one teaching: the One, the Name, the turning from ego toward the Guru. Sikhs hear that oneness in the shared signature, Nanak. Sikhs speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru, the way a lamp lights a lamp. The flame looks different in each lamp. It's the same flame. One teaching, many voices.
screen: `ANGAD: SHORT AND SHARP.` · `AMAR DAS AND RAM DAS: LIGHT, KITCHEN, CITY.` · `ARJAN AND THE NINTH: SWEET, LEVEL, REMAINING.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP TO LAMP.` · then, large: `ONE TEACHING, MANY VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one voice you'll return to. Settle, and breathe. Let the five Gurus pass by, one at a time, like singers taking turns. Guru Angad, short and sharp. Guru Amar Das, the open kitchen. Guru Ram Das, the morning. Guru Arjan, sweetness. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the level heart. Notice which voice you lean toward. There's no wrong answer. Name it quietly to yourself, and hold one line of theirs that you'll come back to. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
The Gurus' teachings close. From the second Guru to the fifth, and the ninth: different voices, one signature, one teaching. Today's word.

Your line: one teaching, many voices. Today, say the line you chose once out loud, and notice the name signed at the end of it: Nanak. Next, we open the tenth Guru's writings. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib each Guru's hymns carry a Mahala heading with a number, and are signed Nanak; Sikhs read and sing them together as one Guru's word.
